newsitem.title: USA: U.S. CREDIT OUTLOOK -- CPI takes center stage.
newsitem.headline: U.S. CREDIT OUTLOOK -- CPI takes center stage.

text.p: U.S. credit markets will scrutinize a key consumer price indicator Wednesday for clues that may hint at what kind of action the Federal Reserve may take at its March policy-setting meeting.
"Tomorrow (Wednesday) will be inflation data day. The whole market will be looking for the numbers and their possible implications on policy," said a trader at a U.S. investment bank.
The government will release the Consumer Price Index (CPI) for February at 0830 EST/1330 GMT.

In a Reuters poll, economists see overall CPI up 0.2 percent in February. The core CPI, which excludes food and energy price fluctuations, is also seen up 0.2 percent. Both, overall and core CPI rose 0.1 percent in January.
Analysts said the consumer price data are expected to confirm the current status of the U.S. economy -- moderate to firm growth with low inflation.

"The CPI will probably set the tone ... The numbers should confirm the good news that we saw last week in the PPI (Producer Price Index) data," said Christopher Low, senior economist at HSBC Markets Inc.
Low was referring to very friendly PPI data released last week which showed overall producer prices dropped 0.4 percent in February.
The senior economist said, however, that U.S. money market still appears to be in a bearish mood and even a friendly CPI may not be enough to boost prices.

"The market is going to be happy with the report ... (but) I think the upside potential for bonds is limited," HSBC's Low said. "I don't think this is going to be a real earth-shaking report," he added.
The CPI release gained even more momentum as players braced for the March 25 meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee, the policy-setting branch of the U.S. central bank.
The market is divided on whether or not the Federal Reserve will move to raise its target for the federal funds rate, currently set at 5.25 percent.

On Wednesday, the market will also be looking at a speech by Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan, who will discuss financial services modernization in a testimony to the Capital Markets, Securities and Government Sponsored Enterprises subcommittee of the House Banking and Financial Services Committee. The event is scheduled for 1000 EST/1500 GMT.

Traders said they do not expect Greenspan to add much to his recent comments about monetary policy made during his Humphrey-Hawkins testimony, when he said the Fed could not rule out a rate hike as a preemptive strike against inflation.
Although it remains a close call, some analysts said that they believe the FOMC will leave rates unchanged in March mostly due to a positive inflation outlook.

"We think the precursors of inflation, like the vendor deliveries and the ECI (employment cost index) data are on their way up," said Dana Saporta, economist at Stone and McCarthy Research Associates Inc.
"But they still are not showing clear enough signals of rising inflation pressures to warrant a tightening right now," Saporta added.
The benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury bond ended down 2/32 at 95-25/32 on Tuesday. Its yield closed at 6.96 percent, unchanged from Monday's close.

The Fed added temporary reserves to the system on Tuesday through a round of overnight system repurchase agreements. Federal funds are seen opening at 5.19 percent on Wednesday, below the Fed's target for the rate.
